1|# Body
2|
3|Onboard software for a differential-drive robot chassis: independent Python processes on a Raspberry Pi (target) communicate over [Zenoh](https://zenoh.io/) using JSON messages. The contract with the desktop agent (Jill / Cognitive Workbench) is defined in [body_project_spec.md](body_project_spec.md).
4|
5|## Requirements
6|
7|- Python 3.11+
8|- `eclipse-zenoh` and, for `oakd_driver`, `depthai` (see [requirements.txt](requirements.txt)); Linux udev rules for Movidius (`03e7`) are required to open the OAK from a non-root user.
9|- **OAK-D-Lite IMU:** retail units usually include a BNO IMU; DepthAI may require `oakd.imu_enable_firmware_update: true` (default in [config.json](config.json)) on first use. Some **Kickstarter OAK-D-Lite** boards have **no IMU** ([Luxonis docs](https://docs.luxonis.com/software-v3/depthai/depthai-components/nodes/imu/)) — set **`imu_hardware_present`: false** to run `oakd_driver` with synthetic `body/oakd/imu` so the launcher does not crash.
10|- A Zenoh **router** (`zenohd`) reachable by every Body process and every client (teleop or Jill). On the robot, run the router on the Pi and listen on TCP **7447** (see [Configuration](#configuration)).
11|
12|## Install (once per machine)
13|
14|Use the **repository root** (the directory that contains `config.json` and the `body/` package—not the inner `body/` folder alone):
15|
16|bash
17|cd /path/to/Body
18|python3 -m venv .venv
19|.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
20|export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)"
21|
22|
23|Use the same `PYTHONPATH` for `launcher`, `teleop`, and any `python -m body.*` command. The launcher also sets `PYTHONPATH` for child processes.
24|
25|## Configuration
26|
27|| Item | Purpose |
28||------|---------|
29|| [config.json](config.json) | Zenoh `connect_endpoints`, motor/lidar/oakd/watchdog tuning. |
30|| `ZENOH_CONNECT` | Optional override: single endpoint, e.g. `tcp/192.168.1.50:7447`. Replaces `zenoh.connect_endpoints` for all processes. |
31|
32|Router on the Pi (matches the spec): listen on `0.0.0.0:7447` so peers on the LAN can connect. Example `zenohd` config fragment:
33|
34|
35|{
36|  "mode": "router",
37|  "listen": { "endpoints": ["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"] }
38|}
39|
40|
41|Processes on the Pi should connect to **`tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`** (default in `config.json`). A laptop running teleop uses **`tcp/<pi-ip>:7447`** via `ZENOH_CONNECT` or edited `connect_endpoints`.
42|
43|### Starting `zenohd` (router)
44|
45|Body expects a **router** already running before you start `body.launcher` or `teleop`.
46|
47|**`zenohd` is not installed by `pip` or your `.venv`.** The Python package `eclipse-zenoh` is only the client library. If the shell says `zenohd: command not found`, install the router binary below (or add it to your `PATH`).
48|
49|1. **Install the router binary** on the machine that runs the router (usually the Pi). Pick one:
50|   - Official options: [Zenoh installation](https://zenoh.io/docs/getting-started/installation/).
51|   - **Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit):** use the **aarch64 Linux standalone** archive from [eclipse-zenoh/zenoh releases](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/releases). Unpack so `zenohd` and the bundled `*.so` plugins stay in the **same directory** (the archive layout is flat). Example (adjust `ZV` to match your `eclipse-zenoh` major.minor, e.g. `1.9.0`):
52|
53|bash
54|ZV=1.9.0
55|curl -sLO "https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh/releases/download/${ZV}/zenoh-${ZV}-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu-standalone.zip"
56|mkdir -p "$HOME/zenoh/${ZV}"
57|unzip -o "zenoh-${ZV}-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu-standalone.zip" -d "$HOME/zenoh/${ZV}"
58|
59|
60|2. **Config:** This repo includes [deploy/zenohd-router.json](deploy/zenohd-router.json) — listens on **TCP `0.0.0.0:7447`**.
61|
62|3. **Run** from the directory that contains `zenohd` (foreground; use `tmux` / `systemd` for production). Example if Body lives at `~/Body`:
63|
64|bash
65|"$HOME/zenoh/1.9.0/zenohd" -c "$HOME/Body/deploy/zenohd-router.json"
66|
67|
68|To put `zenohd` on your `PATH`, copy **both** `zenohd` and the `libzenoh_plugin_*.so` files into the same target directory (e.g. `$HOME/zenoh/1.9.0` already does), then:
69|
70|bash
71|export PATH="$HOME/zenoh/1.9.0:$PATH"
72|zenohd -c "$HOME/Body/deploy/zenohd-router.json"
73|
74|
75|If your `zenohd` build only accepts JSON5 configs, copy `zenohd-router.json` to `zenohd-router.json5` and pass that path.
76|
77|4. **Check:** With `zenohd` running, start `body.launcher` on the Pi; processes should connect to `tcp/127.0.0.1:7447` per [config.json](config.json).
78|
79|## Operation overview
80|
81|mermaid
82|flowchart LR
83|  subgraph pi [Pi]
84|    R[zenohd]
85|    L[body.launcher]
86|    R --- L
87|  end
88|  subgraph clients [Clients optional]
89|    T[body.teleop]
90|    J[Jill bridge]
91|  end
92|  T --> R
93|  J --> R
94|
95|
96|1. Start **`zenohd`** on the Pi (or your dev box for all-local tests).
97|2. Start **`body.launcher`** on the Pi (motor, lidar, oakd, watchdog processes).
98|3. Optionally start **`body.teleop`** or a Jill-side bridge so **`body/heartbeat`** and **`body/cmd_vel`** are published. Without heartbeats, the watchdog will treat the robot as not under command and can trigger **`body/emergency_stop`**.
99|
100|## Running the stack (`body.launcher`)
101|
102|On the **Pi** (after `zenohd` is up):
103|
104|bash
105|cd /path/to/Body
106|export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)"
107|.venv/bin/python -m body.launcher
108|
109|
110|Startup order: `watchdog` → `motor_controller` → `lidar_driver` → `oakd_driver`. Logs are prefixed by process name.
111|
112|**Stop:** `Ctrl+C` or `SIGTERM` to the launcher; it sends `SIGTERM` to children, waits, then `SIGKILL` if needed.
113|
114|**Restarts:** If a child exits unexpectedly, the launcher restarts it with exponential backoff (capped at 30 s).
115|
116|**Deploy tip:** If errors reference old line numbers or missing symbols (e.g. `XLinkOut` on DepthAI v3), the Pi’s `~/Body` tree is behind your main repo—`git pull` or rsync the updated `body/` tree, then restart the launcher.
117|
118|**Watchdog:** Until something publishes **`body/heartbeat`** (e.g. `body.teleop`), the watchdog may emit **`body/emergency_stop`** (`heartbeat_timeout`). That is expected; start teleop or another client when you want the stack to see a live operator.
119|
120|## Standalone mode (no Jill)
121|
122|**Standalone** means: Body processes on the Pi, and **you** provide heartbeat and velocity commands using the repo’s teleop client—Cognitive Workbench does not need to run.
123|
124|### On the Pi
125|
126|1. Start `zenohd`.
127|2. Start `body.launcher` as above.
128|
129|### On the same Pi (keyboard / SSH session on robot)
130|
131|bash
132|cd /path/to/Body
133|export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)"
134|.venv/bin/python -m body.teleop
135|
136|
137|Default `config.json` uses `tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`, which matches a local router.
138|
139|### On a laptop / workstation (robot’s router on LAN)
140|
141|Point Zenoh at the Pi:
142|
143|bash
144|cd /path/to/Body
145|export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)"
146|export ZENOH_CONNECT=tcp/192.168.1.50:7447
147|.venv/bin/python -m body.teleop
148|
149|
150|(Replace the address with your Pi’s IP or hostname.)
151|
152|### Teleop REPL
153|
154|| Command | Meaning |
155||---------|---------|
156|| `vel LINEAR [ANGULAR]` | Latch `body/cmd_vel`: linear m/s, angular rad/s (CCW positive). Angular defaults to `0`. |
157|| `stop` | Latch zero velocity. |
158|| `status` | Print last `body/status` JSON (if any). |
159|| `help` | Short help. |
160|| `quit` / `q` | Exit teleop (heartbeat and cmd_vel stop; robot may e-stop if nothing else publishes heartbeat). |
161|
162|Optional flags: `--heartbeat-hz` (default 2), `--cmd-vel-hz` (default 20), `--timeout-ms` (default 500), `--verbose` (print every `body/status`).
163|
164|**Motion authority:** Do **not** run teleop and another publisher (e.g. Jill) both commanding `body/cmd_vel` at the same time; the motor side effectively sees interleaved commands.

300|**Loop structure:**
301|- Main loop at 50 Hz (20ms cycle).
302|- Each cycle: read encoders → compute odometry → check for cmd timeout → compute PWM from latest command → write GPIO → publish odom and motor_state.

305|**Differential drive math:**
306|
307|wheel_base = W  (meters, measured)
308|wheel_radius = R  (meters, measured)
309|

311|  v_left  = v - (ω * W / 2)
312|  v_right = v + (ω * W / 2)

462|The following assumptions apply to the desktop agent (Jill / CW) and are **out of scope** for this project but must be satisfied for the system to function:

464|1. **Zenoh connectivity.** The desktop must connect to the Zenoh router running on the Pi at `tcp://<pi-ip>:7447`. This may require a new Zenoh session configuration in the CW infrastructure or a new "robot" tool/skill that manages the connection.
465|
466|2. **Heartbeat publication.** Jill (or a CW-side robot interface module) must publish `body/heartbeat` at ≥2 Hz whenever she expects the robot to be active. If she stops publishing, the robot stops moving. This is by design.
467|
468|3. **Command publication.** Jill publishes `body/cmd_vel` to drive the robot. She is responsible for rate-limiting her own commands sensibly (10–20 Hz is reasonable). She must respect the timeout semantics — if she wants the robot to keep moving, she must keep publishing.
